Because I am a cook. I am a true professional.
Really? Attention everyone in the kitchen!
A great cook has come to us!
We waited for him for so long!
There is a special job for you!

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order
the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

examples.text: Давай работай быстрее, гости уже давно ждут заказ!
examples.trans: Come on, work faster, the guests have been waiting for their order for a long time!

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('great').
Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Прошу внимания = May I have your attention
Russian preposition meaning 'around' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: She was running after me (around me).
She circled around me like a shark.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to cook; to prepare', paired with 'приготовить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to prepare') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я уже не могу готовить, стирать, убирать. Я хочу на море!
examples.trans: I can't take the cooking, washing and cleaning any more. I want to go to the sea!

meanings.note: usually the short form: я готов (m), я готова (f)
emphatic at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('? = really?, oh yeah?') (disbelief) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to make') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: We could open a salon for you.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: He talks for a long time.
We'll make it! The president always talks for a long time.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to wait', forming an aspectual pair with 'подождать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to expect') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'пойти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('expression') (to run for a second term) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'to' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('what') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
in exclamations: какой грязный! = how dirty!

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'any', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Любая обезьяна эти выборы выиграет! Ты что, хуже обезьяны?
examples.trans: Any monkey will win this election! What, are you worse than a monkey?

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'стоящий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('real, genuine').
Secondary conversational sense ('present, current') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ваня, да пойми ты наконец! Это настоящий успех.
examples.trans: Vanya, understand at last! This is real success.

meanings.note: hesitation, at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('oh come on!') (ну, папа!) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: accusative/genitive его (него after prepositions), dative ему (нему)
Secondary conversational sense ('it') (for masculine and neuter things) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'special' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.

examples.text: Такие люди должны лежать в особенном месте!
examples.trans: Such people should lie in a special place!
Today is a special day for us.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'пере-' denotes crossing over, repeating, or exceeding a limit (stem 'одеваться'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to get changed', forming an aspectual pair with 'переодеться'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.trans: Quickly change clothes, let's get to work!

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'cook', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.en: to have a look, to take a look
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'смотреть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to have a look', forming an aspectual pair with 'смотреть'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to watch (a film) through') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'that's why'.
Secondary conversational sense ('that's why') (потому и = that's exactly why) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я устал, потому что много работал.
examples.trans: I'm tired because I worked a lot.
I'm at home because I'm ill.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'why'.

examples.trans: Why are we going so slowly?

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to come', forming an aspectual pair with 'приходить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Security will be here any moment.

examples.text: Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
examples.trans: Don't, Samson. Security will be here any second.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'фессионал'). Common masculine noun meaning 'professional' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: У вас тут в провинции одни профессионалы.
examples.trans: You've got nothing but professionals out here in the provinces.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'work', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('job') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.

examples.trans: The white one? Give me the keys.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('like that, so') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('I have') (possession) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('from (ask from someone)') (просить у кого) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

уметь.gloss: to know how to, to be able to

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'меть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to know how to', forming an aspectual pair with 'суметь'.

examples.text: Эх, Паша, Паша. Ты считать не умеешь.
examples.trans: Oh, Pasha, Pasha. You can't count.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'well'.
Secondary conversational sense ('good, fine') (as an answer) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Хорошо, Виктор Петрович, я сейчас же всё переделаю заново!
examples.trans: All right, Viktor Petrovich, I will redo everything right now!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
